observations.topic: Undergraduate problems are judged too long or confusing when the sequence includes events beyond the core textbook transformation (a preliminary or follow-up step, or a further reaction of a reagent-derived fragment).
observations.proposal: Add a rule for the undergraduate level: the problem covers one textbook transformation; a preliminary or follow-up operation (e.g. a saponification before the key step, or hydrolysis of the product of the key step) is left out unless it is part of the same named textbook reaction.

observations.topic: Advanced problems whose sequence consists mainly of protecting-group removal or hydrolysis are judged too easy or better suited to a lower level.
observations.proposal: Add a rule for the advanced level: at least half of the difficulty score must come from specialized steps and uncommon reagents, and a problem whose specialized character rests on a deprotection or hydrolysis step is not used at that level.

observations.topic: A graduate problem with a multi-step rearrangement sequence and an uncommon reagent was judged too hard for the graduate level.
Advanced problems whose product differs little from the substrate (small structural change, common reagents) are judged too easy.
observations.proposal: Add a rule for the advanced level: the product must differ from the substrate by at least two skeletal bonds (C–C or ring C–heteroatom bonds made or broken, protecting-group atoms not counted), so that a one-site reduction or deprotection cannot carry an advanced problem.

observations.topic: In graduate and advanced problems, undergraduate-level steps (deprotection, acetal hydrolysis) are felt to add work without difficulty; solvers suggest not asking for their intermediates or not counting them in the difficulty.
observations.proposal: Change the advanced-level shape rule: an undergraduate-level step (deprotection, hydrolysis, work-up) may be part of the sequence but does not count toward the minimum of 2 steps, and its intermediates are optional (shown after solving rather than required).

observations.topic: Ratings of advanced problems are low overall.
observations.proposal: For the advanced level, require that specialized steps and uncommon reagents provide at least two thirds of the difficulty score (undergraduate steps contributing at most one third), so that advanced problems rest on the specialized chemistry that was rated well (4 stars for the Pd-catalysed ring expansion).

observations.topic: Ratings of graduate problems average about 3 (lower than undergraduate problems), pulled down by one long multi-step graduate problem with an uncommon reagent.
observations.proposal: Set an upper limit for the graduate difficulty score (for example 7) and no uncommon reagent at the graduate level, so that graduate problems stay below the advanced level in complexity.

observations.topic: Undergraduate problems built on one core textbook transformation with a short, direct sequence of intermediates receive the highest ratings, with solvers praising their clarity and level.
observations.proposal: Add to the selection rules of the procedure a preference for undergraduate problems consisting of one core textbook transformation whose intermediates all belong to that transformation (no preliminary deprotection, separate work-up step or further reaction of a reagent-derived fragment); this is the positive counterpart of the earlier proposal undergraduate-problems-include-extra-steps and could be decided together with it.
